text.p: Investors should exercise caution when considering Swedish bonds, as domestic politics and concerns over a possible delay to the start of EMU would continue to upset the market, analysts said on Thursday.
The Swedish/German 10-year yield gap would likely shrink after the impending federal budget, but analysts saw it swelling longer term.
"The market will remain extremely volatile over the coming months," said James McKay, international economist at PaineWebber in London.
"There will be opportunities, but there will be further set backs as well," he said.

The market recieved a fillip earlier when the Riksbank issued it's quarterly inflation report saying Swedish inflation would remain low and not ruling out a further cut in interest rates at some point.
A trader at a Scandinavian bank in London said the report held no surprises and some confidence was coming back into the short end of the market, around the two-year sector.
"That confidence seems to have spread out along the curve," he said. "We have now got the spread over Germany down, where on a week we peaked at 160."
At 1144 GMT the 10-year Swedish/German spread was at 148 basis points compared with 83 at the beginning of the year.
The trader said during the week there had been swings in the spread of 20 basis points.

"If you have managed to stay in with these swings then stay on," he said. "You are still going to see some volatility in the spread, but some people are returning to the market. But I would certainly put an air of caution on it."
He said it was not the time to invest large ammounts, but rather a time to start building.
McKay said following the budget, on April 15, spreads were likely to converge but on a 12 month view he saw spreads stretching to 200 basis points as the Swedish election loomed.
Wike Groenenberg, European economist at Salomon Brothers International in London, also said once fiscal concerns abated the spread would go back down to around 100 basis points.

"The April 15 finance bill could be a trigger," she said. "It will take away some of the uncertainties in the market and clarify the fiscal policy stance of the government, thus icreasing confidence in the Swedish market."

But, she said uncertainties surrounding European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would not disappear as quickly. Some analysts said EMU concerns were not affecting Sweden as much as Italy and Spain because Sweden was not expected to participate in the first round. But Groenenberg said it was significant to the Swedish market.
"Some investors are of the opinion that if you don't have the EMU stick behind the door Swedish fiscal policy makers may be more willing to spend money," she said.
McKay pointed to the government's suggestion to introduce a 10 billion crown ($1.3 billion) jobs package in the April 15 budget.
"Over the next 18 months we will see further moves to try and regain public support by spending more cash and clearly this is worrying the market," he said.
Analysts said investors should remain cautious at the longer-end of the Swedish market but at the shorter end, the two-year sector looked particularly favourable.

The Scandinavian bank trader said there were few worries at the short end of the market and although currency weakness would seep into the economy at some point, it would mainly affect the export sector. But he remained cautious.
"When panic comes into the market then all the fundamental issues go straight out of the window as we have seen this week."
